prompt: what is a haiku
reply:
Three lines, no rhyme needed. You count syllables instead: five, seven, five 🍃. Clap once per syllable and you will hear them, like this:
[POEM]Rain on the hot road,
steam rises for one minute,
then the smell arrives.[/POEM]
Clap the middle line out loud 👏
[QUIZ]How many claps did the middle line take?[/QUIZ]
[CHIPS]Five|Seven|Nine[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write a limerick
reply:
A limerick is five lines with a bouncy beat 🎪. Lines one, two and five are longer and rhyme together; lines three and four are short and rhyme with each other 🎯
[STEPS]Pick a funny character|Rhyme lines one, two and five|Keep lines three and four short|Save the surprise for the end[/STEPS]
Start with the character. Who is it?
[CHIPS]A greedy goat|My maths textbook|A runaway auto[/CHIPS]

prompt: why do songs have a chorus
reply:
Because a song has to be learnable in one listen 🎧. The verses move the story along; the chorus is the part that stays the same, so your brain has something to grab. That is also why the chorus often carries the title 🔁
[FACT]Songs were passed on by singing long before writing existed.[/FACT]

prompt: what is free verse and is it just lazy writing
reply:
Fair suspicion, but no. Free verse drops rhyme and fixed metre, then has to earn your attention another way: line breaks, repetition, image, silence. Rhyme hands you a skeleton, free verse means building one, which is harder to fake because there is nothing to hide behind 📖. Read one aloud and watch where the line breaks make you pause, that pause is the technique.
[CHIPS]Show me line breaks|Is haiku free verse|Try one on me[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write a poem that doesn't sound cheesy

Swap each feeling-word for the object, gesture or smell that caused it, and let the reader do the feeling ✍️. Try it on your weakest line and send it back to me.

prompt: how do rappers fit so many syllables into one line
reply:
They are not stretching the bar, they are subdividing it. The beat stays at four counts, and the words split those counts into smaller pieces, so more syllables ride the same amount of time. They also lean on internal rhyme, rhyming inside the line rather than only at the end, so your ear keeps finding landmarks 🎤. Tap four steady counts and say both rows at the same speed:
[POEM]one, two, three, four
one-and-a, two-and-a, three-and-a, four[/POEM]
[CHIPS]What is internal rhyme|Try a slow bar|Why four counts[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is iambic pentameter
reply:
Five pairs of syllables per line, each pair going soft-LOUD ⏱️. It sits close to the way English already stresses words, which is why Shakespeare could write whole plays in it without them sounding sung. Good poets break the pattern deliberately, exactly where they want you to notice. Say this one out loud and you have heard the shape:
[POEM]da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM
the CLOCK aBOVE the DOOR is RUNning SLOW[/POEM]
[CHIPS]Count mine with me|Why break the pattern|Other metres[/CHIPS]

prompt: my poem ending feels flat how do i fix it

Better to end on an image than a conclusion: the object left on the table, not the lesson learned 🔍. Here the third line is the one to cut, and you can feel why:
[POEM]The kite is in the neem tree still.
I walk home slower than I came.
That is how it feels to lose something.[/POEM]

prompt: how do songwriters come up with a hook
reply:
Mostly by accident, then by ruthless editing. A hook is the shortest phrase that survives being repeated twenty times, so writers hum nonsense over a chord loop until one shape refuses to leave 🎶
[STEPS]Hum a loop with no words|Keep the shape that will not leave|Fit real words to that exact rhythm|Test it twenty times out loud[/STEPS]
Hooks tend to use short, open vowel sounds, because those are easy to sing loudly. Hum four notes now and find words that match 🎵
[CHIPS]Explain chord loops|Try humming first|Why open vowels[/CHIPS]

prompt: whats the actual difference between a poem and song lyrics
reply:
Lyrics are built to be incomplete. Much of the emotional work is done by melody, rhythm and a human voice, so lyrics on paper can look plain and still be excellent. A poem has to carry all of that alone, using only marks on a page 🎧. Read a lyric you love with no tune in your head and you will feel exactly what the music was holding up.
[CHIPS]Test a lyric flat|Can lyrics be poems|Write one of each[/CHIPS]

prompt: does a poem have to rhyme to be taken seriously
reply:
No, and much of the published poetry in English over the last century has not rhymed. Rhyme is a tool: it binds lines, helps memory and signals play, which is why it rules songs, jokes and verse for small children. Serious writing needs structure, not rhyme specifically 🎯. Rhyme when it earns its place, and drop it the moment you catch yourself choosing a worse word to hit the sound.
[CHIPS]When rhyme helps|Slant rhyme instead|Test my rhyming poem[/CHIPS]

prompt: what is a slant rhyme
reply:
A rhyme that almost lands: home and come, shape and shop 🎧. The consonants or the vowels match, but not both, so your ear registers a near miss instead of a click. Writers reach for it when a perfect rhyme would sound too neat for the subject, and Emily Dickinson built much of her work on it. Replace one perfect rhyme in your poem with a slant one and listen to what changes.
[CHIPS]Slant rhymes for night|Why it sounds unfinished|Perfect versus slant[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i write for a poetry competition without accidentally copying someone
reply:
The real risk is lines you half-remember, so draft with no poems open, then check any phrase that arrived too easily. If it sounded finished before you worked on it, it may not be yours. Borrowing a form, such as a sonnet or a villanelle, is never copying; borrowing images and phrasing is ✍️. Ground the poem in something only you have seen, your street, your grandmother's kitchen, and the overlap mostly disappears.
[CHIPS]Check a suspect line|What counts as form|Find my own material[/CHIPS]

prompt: how do i make my lyrics fit the tune i already have
reply: Count the tune before you write a word: hum it and mark where the stressed beats fall, then write lines whose natural stresses land on those beats. If a word fights the tune you will hear it, because one syllable gets stretched or swallowed. Fix it by changing the word rather than the melody 🎹.
